Egg diameter in Novaculichthys taeniourus has been estimated at 0.8 millimeters, a dimension from which the wet weight of individual eggs at the moment of fertilization can be calculated using the volumetric formula for a sphere. Assuming neutral buoyancy in seawater, the resulting wet weight at birth is approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams], a remarkably small initial mass that places the early offspring squarely within the pelagic egg size range typical of many labrids. These minute, transparent eggs are broadcast into the water column during the twilight hours, where they undergo rapid embryonic development driven by the ambient thermal regime. The duration of the embryonic period is brief, with the age at birth, defined as the interval from oviposition to eclosion of the yolk-sac larva, lasting 3.6 days [ab = 3.6 days] when maintained at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This swift hatching time, consistent with the rapid developmental rates observed in other tropical reef fishes, minimizes the window of vulnerability to benthic egg predators but exposes the newly emerged prolarvae to the intense predation pressure characteristic of planktonic environments.

Following the transition to the pelagic larval phase, the growing individual of Novaculichthys taeniourus proceeds along a growth trajectory that ultimately defines its asymptotic body size. The ultimate total length, representing the maximum size an individual can attain under favorable environmental conditions, is 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters]. This relatively modest terminal length, compared to some of the larger labrids such as the humphead wrasse Cheilinus undulatus which can exceed two meters, reflects the rockmover wrasse's specialized morphology as an inhabitant of rubble and sand flats where it uses its pectoral fins to overturn stones and coral fragments in search of cryptic prey. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, which represents the maximum adult body mass predicted by the length-weight relationship for this species, is approximately 31 grams [Wwp = approximately 31 grams]. This value, derived from an allometric scaling equation applied to the ultimate length, suggests a relatively slender body form consistent with the species' active foraging lifestyle, wherein excess mass would impair maneuverability among the complex reef substrate.

The onset of reproductive capability in Novaculichthys taeniourus is marked by the attainment of a specific body size, known as the total length at puberty, which has been determined to be 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters]. This size threshold corresponds to the point at which the gonads begin vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis, initiating the transition from an immature, non-reproductive juvenile to a potentially breeding adult. The associated wet weight at puberty, calculated from the length-weight relationship for individuals of this length, is approximately 470 grams [Wwi = approximately 470 grams]. Interestingly, this mass is substantially larger than the ultimate wet weight, a seeming paradox that arises because the length-weight relationship is an allometric power function that does not incorporate the asymptotic plateau in growth; in practice, individuals do not typically achieve both the weight at puberty and the ultimate length simultaneously, as growth decelerates markedly after maturity. Puberty in this species is reached relatively early in the maximal lifespan, allowing several years of reproductive activity before senescence begins.

Longevity in the Rockmover wrasse has been inferred from comparative data on the closely related cuckoo wrasse Centrolabrus exoletus, given the lack of direct age-validation studies for Novaculichthys taeniourus. Under the environmental conditions typical of tropical coral reef habitats, where water temperatures average around 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], the maximum lifespan is estimated to be 8 years [am = 8 years]. This lifespan, equivalent to 2920 days, represents a moderate duration among Indo-Pacific labrids, many of which exhibit lifespans ranging from 3 to 15 years depending on body size and predation regime. The warm, stable thermal environment likely accelerates metabolic rates and cellular aging processes compared to temperate confamilials, yet the species' relatively small body size and high natural mortality from piscivorous predators may select against the evolution of extreme longevity. Field studies employing otolith microchemistry or mark-recapture techniques would be valuable for verifying whether captive-derived estimates accurately reflect wild population demographics.
